::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Replication studies are essential for building cumulative knowledge in second language acquisition (SLA) research because they allow researchers to revisit, contextualize, and extend the findings of earlier studies.
Rather than arguing for the value of replication, this chapter focuses on the replication research process itself.
It begins with two core issues: deciding what study to replicate and what kind of replication to conduct (conceptual, approximate, close, or exact).
It then considers the place of replication in qualitative research.

The chapter reviews methodological considerations for planning a replication, supported by a set of planning questions, and for disseminating it through presentations and journal articles, including reporting standards.
It then describes the practical relevance of replication for building confidence in findings before they are applied and for testing lab-based results in classrooms.

The chapter closes with future directions: integrating replication into research programs, extending it beyond quantitative methods, improving planning and reporting, and adopting open research practices.

text.text: However, because questions about the relevance and potential value of replication are now behind us, this chapter centers on the replication research process itself.
As I see it, improving how we plan, conduct, and disseminate replication research is where our attention and effort is most required today.
To this end, I begin with two core issues that are pivotal to the success of a replication research project: decisions about what to replicate and what kind of replication study to conduct.
I also discuss replication in the context of qualitative methods.
I then review replication methodology with a focus on planning and dissemination.
This chapter concludes by reviewing the practical relevance and future of replication research in SLA research.
One of the biggest challenges at the beginning of a replication research project involves deciding what prior study to replicate.

text.text: A study should not be replicated just because it has not yet been replicated.
Similarly, a study that has been replicated before can be replicated again (for examples, see McManus et al., 2026; Morgan-Short et al., 2018).

text.text: Consistent with all types of research, a replication study should be motivated based on its potential contribution to knowledge and not the absence of research alone.

Turning attention to some of the reasons that might favor the selection of a study to be replicated, Porte and McManus (2019) recommended researchers to consider the following factors: (a) value/impact, (b) continued relevance, (c) access to data and materials, (c) unexpected or unusual results, and (d) statistical and methodological rigor (see also Isager et al., 2023; Marsden et al., 2018; McManus, 2024a).

text.text: Based on this, studies that are valuable and impactful for the field (e.g., theory, academic, social) and relevant today represent a good starting point.
In addition, researchers should determine if their identified study provides access to the data and materials.
It is extremely difficult to replicate a study without access to the materials.
Developing new materials from scratch can also introduce new sources of error and variation in study outcomes, thus preventing a clear comparison to the initial study.
Access to data is becoming increasingly important to draw meaningful comparisons between studies (see McManus et al., 2025).

text.text: Researchers should also review the candidate study for its findings, including whether the results are unexpected, surprising and/or they appear inconsistent with the rest of the field.
Lastly, methodological rigor is an important consideration as well.

text.text: Although labels such as "exact", "direct", "partial", "systematic" exist, they are less common today in SLA.
We can think about these different kinds of replication studies in terms of (a) amounts of intentional change and (b) the aims of the replication study.
We will review these different kinds of replication, starting with conceptual, followed by approximate and close, and then exact.
We will see that each type of replication is defined in terms of its comparability with the initial study and its aims.

The label "conceptual replication" is likely the most familiar. Schmidt (2009) defines conceptual replications as the "repetition of a test of a hypothesis or a result of earlier research work with different methods" (p. 91).

text.text: From a quantitative methods perspective, we can think of conceptual replications as a way to revisit the internal and construct validity of a finding by modifying the study's operationalizations of key theoretical concepts (Finkel et al., 2017; Nosek & Errington, 2020; Slough & Tyson, 2024).

text.text: In this way, conceptual replications address the same research question(s) as the initial study, but often by using different methods.

In this way, Wu and Fricke's conceptual replication intentionally varied the study's core constructs to investigate the extent to which Jacob's findings applied to a different kind of L1-L2 pairings (Chinese-English vs.
Russian-German).
Approximate and close replication studies include smaller amounts of modification than conceptual replications when compared to the initial study.
In close/approximate replications, researchers often seek to contribute to the external validity of the initial study's conclusions.

This is achieved by modifying elements of the initial study's procedures (population, contrasts, measurement strategies) to examine the extent to which specific and intentional variations shape the effect of interest.

In other words, close and approximate replications allow us to learn something about the external validity or generalizability of a finding by intentionally modifying specific elements of the initial study's procedures (Finkel et al., 2017; Porte & McManus, 2019; Slough & Tyson, 2024).

text.text: The difference between close and approximate replication concerns the amount of intentional variation integrated into the design.
For example, Ryan et al. (2024) reported a close replication of Tavakoli and Foster's (2008) investigation of narrative task design in L2 oral performance.

text.text: Their close replication varied the L1 literacy level of the learner (advanced in the initial study, and low in the replication) while keeping other aspects of the initial study stable (e.g., L2 proficiency, independent variables, tasks).
In this way, their close replication investigated to what extent the initial study's findings additionally applied to L2 learners with low levels of L1 literacy.

We can contrast this approach with November 5, 2026 Routledge Handbook of Second Language Acquisition Kevin McManus, kevin.mcmanus@pitt.edu approximate replication where up to two key variables of interest are modified in the replication (e.g., population and task).
Pelzl et al. (2024), for example, conducted an approximate replication of Van Hell and Dijkstra (2002) in which two variables were modified.
First, the population was modified to include Dutch-English bilinguals whereas the initial study included Dutch-English-French trilinguals.
Second, the replication study was conducted online whereas the initial study was conducted in a lab.
All other aspects of the initial study were retained and not intentionally modified.

In this way, the replication examined to what extent the initial study's findings extended to (a) a different population, (i.e., bilinguals vs. trilinguals) and (b) differences in data collection modality.
The last approach to replication reviewed here is exact replication, in which the exact procedures of the initial study are precisely repeated without modification.
The research aim goal in exact replication is to ascertain the replicability of the initial result.
That is, to what extent does exactly and precisely repeating the initial study's method produce the same result?
This approach of replication is not possible in SLA and is presented for information.
We cannot exactly repeat a previous study's method without there being modifications since in SLA we study people (Guttinger, 2020; Schmidt, 2009) and people are complex and time-variant.

In the preceding sections, I introduced replication as a process of doing research to better understand prior studies that have been impactful (e.g., academically, theoretically, socially).
To what extent is replication a viable, appropriate, and useful research method in empirical studies using qualitative methods?

In general, replication has not really been encouraged in qualitative research and is often seen as incompatible with the foundational assumptions of qualitative research (Casanave, 2012; Markee, 2017; Porte & Richards, 2012; Willig, 2019).
text.formatted: In general, replication has not really been encouraged in qualitative research and is often seen as incompatible with the foundational assumptions of qualitative research <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Casanave, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Markee, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Porte & Richards, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Willig, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: There are several reasons for this position, including differing positions on "truth", reality, interpretation and researcher subjectivity.
Interpretation, for example, is a key tool in qualitative research, which is informed by the researcher's stance and their approach to interpretation.
Pownall (2024) argues that subjectivity and positionality are so intentional and inherent to the

text.text: In addition, qualitative research often aims to study "exceptional phenomena" (Tuval-Mashiach, 2021, p. 368) in which circumstances appear unique in order to learn about individuals with particularly distinctive qualities or life experiences (Duff, 2025; Sandelowski, 1986).

text.text: Overall, these concerns appear appropriate.
However, I don't think they are unique to qualitative SLA research.
Claims of replication incompatibility are at least partly rooted in a traditional view of replication as referring to exact replication only.
In other words, replications that seek to provide identical findings and context-free generalization (i.e., the replicability aim).
These understandings of replication are (a) rarely practiced in SLA and (b) not achievable (Porte & McManus, 2019).
text.formatted: These understandings of replication are (a) rarely practiced in SLA and (b) not achievable <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Porte & McManus, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Rather, in contemporary SLA, replication refers to the systematic revisiting of one or more aspects of an earlier study (its methods, participants, sites, or claims) in order to corroborate, elaborate, contrast, and clarify.

On this account, the value of qualitative replication lies in clarifying where interpretations converge, diverge, become more differentiated, or reveal their contextual limits, thereby supporting the cumulative development of knowledge.

Indeed, some of the aims of replication research as defined here are related to several important concepts in qualitative research, including transferability, dependability, and confirmability (Bitsch, 2005; Krefting, 1991; Lincoln & Guba, 1985; Markee, 2017).

text.text: First, transferability is the degree to which qualitative research findings can be transferred to other contexts or settings conducted among other respondents.
The focus here is on whether the results of a previous study apply to a new setting.

Second, dependability is November 5, 2026 Routledge Handbook of Second Language Acquisition Kevin McManus, kevin.mcmanus@pitt.edu 11 defined as the stability of findings over time, with the expectation that what should be expected is variability over consistency of findings.
This is because qualitative research emphasizes the uniqueness of the human situation, so that variation in experience rather than identical repetition is sought.
Third, confirmability is defined as the degree to which the findings of study can be confirmed by other researchers and are clearly derived from and embedded in the data.
Indeed, these principles have entered into some proposals for how replication studies can play a role in qualitative research.

Talkad Sukumar & Metoyer (2019) suggest, for example, that a qualitative replication study repeats one of more aspects of a prior study (e.g., methods, participants) and embeds within its findings an interpretive comparison with a view to corroborate, elaborate, contrast, or clarify the elements corresponding to the replicated aspects with those of the earlier study (see also East, 2021; Kim, 2025; Markee, 2017).

text.text: Taken together, replication serves to broaden the perspective of prior findings to facilitate accumulation of knowledge.
In this section, I focus on two components of doing replication research: planning and dissemination.
For each component, I highlight the essential elements key to the conduct of high-quality replication.

text.text: A high-quality replication study is not just repetition of a prior study.
It is a thoughtful process in which we seek to contribute new understanding about a prior result and we do this by revisiting its fundamentals.

We thus need to think carefully about (a) the ongoing relevance and impact of the study selected for replication, (b) what the replication study will look like and why, and (c) anticipated disciplinary gains from doing the replication.
Each one of these questions is nontrivial and will significantly shape the trajectory of the project.
Appendix A includes key questions to assist with planning a replication project (adapted from McManus, 2023).
Section A is about the initial study that you are planning to replicate.
The value of the initial study is essential to the success of your replication project.
Here, you should think about the fundamental importance, relevance, and quality of the study.

For example, has the study been important for a line or research, has it concluded something highly relevant to how and/or what is researched today, are the topics / hypotheses / research questions important and high quality?
Related to study value is impact and this is about the effects that the study has had (e.g., academic, societal).
For example, has the study impacted academic work (e.g., citations), has the study appeared in textbooks and reference manuals, has the study shaped society?

Study value tends to be internal, ongoing, and tied to the process of the research, whereas impact is often external, outcome-driven, and tied November 5, 2026 Routledge Handbook of Second Language Acquisition Kevin McManus, kevin.mcmanus@pitt.edu 13 to the results.
It is important to think about these two factors because we want to select a study for replication that is both valuable and impactful.
Moving on to questions of design, you want to make sure that you understand the initial study.

Section B focuses your attention on these aspects of the initial study, including what the research questions were, what materials, data, and analysis tools are available, where the study was conducted, and who the research participants were.
Understanding these features of the initial study will help you to design a high-quality replication.
Anymore, I don't think it's reasonable to replicate a study without access to the data collection materials.
I also think having access to the initial study's data is becoming increasingly important.
With a solid understanding of the initial study, the next series of questions focus on your replication study.
The aim here is to start thinking about your replication study design and its comparability to the initial study.
For Section C, your aim is to identify whether the variable is (a) the same, (b) close to, or (c) different from the initial study.
Will the replication use the same research materials as the initial, will they be modified, or will the materials be different?
Each question provides you with information about what you are changing.
By answering these replication design questions, you will get an idea about the comparability of your replication in light of the initial study.
The next step is thinking about the value and anticipated impact of your replication.
I include this section because it often gets overlooked.
Here, the focus is on the "so what?"
question before you've carried out the study.
This is imperative when it comes to dissemination (next section).
Section D begins with questions about similarities and differences between the two studies and what type of replication you think the design represents.

These are important because you'll have some genuine differences that are deliberate (e.g., studying learners with different L1 backgrounds) and others that may not be (e.g., conducting the study in 2026).
It is important to be clear about these in advance.
Other questions in this section push you toward thinking about the ways in which your modifications (major, minor, intentional) might influence the results, empirically and conceptually.
Reporting and sharing your replication project are essential parts of doing research too, so we need to build in time for dissemination.
SLA researchers regularly participate in different kinds of dissemination, including conference presentations and journal articles.
These mediums of dissemination are the ones I primarily focus on here.
Giving a presentation about your research is the most recommended and useful first step for dissemination.
Indeed, about 75% of participants in McManus' (2022a) survey of replication practices reported presenting a replication study at a meeting or conference.
While the same recommended practices for presentations hold for replications, there are

text.text: Starting with the abstract, remember to keep the aim of the project clear.
This means explicitly identifying the study as a replication in the title and abstract (McManus, 2024b).
Conference programs still show that we need to keep paying attention to the ways in which replication projects are communicated because many abstract titles still exclude replication.
Appropriately describing the study in title is important for the discoverability and transparency of research.

The abstract too should also incorporate elements of the replication study's aims, including (a) the study that was replicated, (b) the reason/motivation for doing the replication, (c) the modifications made with justifications, and (d) key findings with comparisons to the initial study.
These elements help others to understand and evaluate the study and its contribution to knowledge.
Moving on to the presentation itself (paper or poster), attention to communicating the replication study's aims, research design and methods, findings, and interpretations is still needed.
As discussed earlier, replication is not only a way of collecting data (research method); it is a way of thinking and doing research (methodology).
It is important to be explicit about the study's aims (i.e., why you decided to conduct the replication).
As you go about designing the presentation, here are some features to pay close attention to.

The first part of your presentation will involve discussion of: (a) why you decided to replicate the study, (b) a review of the study to be replicated, and (c) your replication approach including what was modified and why.

Your methods will present the research questions (from the initial study, with modifications, if appropriate) as well as how the data collected and prepared for analysis, drawing comparisons with the initial study.

You will also want to note if you used the same data collection materials and if you had access to the initial study's data and are using it (if you do have access to the initial study's data, please use it in your analysis).
Then, report your results to allow for maximum comparison with the initial study (e.g., tables and visuals with data from both studies).
Make sure you discuss the similarities and differences in the results and how you arrived at those conclusions (i.e., how do you decide if the results are the same or not?).
Of course, this is a non-exhaustive list of practices designed to allow the audience to understand what you did, how you did it, and what you found.
While the same recommendations apply to paper and poster presentations, the way you go about representing this in poster form will look a little different.
For a detailed account for poster presentations of a replication project, see Porte and McManus (2019).

text.text: At the same time, few journals provide guidance to support authors in publishing replication studies (McManus, 2024b).

text.text: These are important observations because replication study reporting includes several features that distinguishes them from most other types of empirical reports (e.g., systematic comparison in how the study is situated, presented; a literature review focused on the study being replicated).

For this reason, an essential resource for authors are the reporting standards for replication studies in applied linguistics (McManus, 2024b), which outlines minimum reporting expectations for replication studies (see also Porte & McManus, 2019).

text.text: This reporting standard includes author guidance for the features to be included in each section of the manuscript.
This is an important addition to the literature to address publishing challenges for replication studies.
In many instances, a challenge with publishing a replication study tends to be found in how the study is presented and motivated.
This replication standard outlines ways to communicate the specific aims of the study.
As the SSLA special issue on replication studies shows, there are some important differences that need to be attended to when reporting a replication study in journal articles (see McManus, 2024a).
As with any research, a challenge to publication can be that the authors have not provided a compelling motivation for why the study was carried out.
This applies to replication research too.
This section reviews the ways in which replication studies are relevant to instruction and other domains such as assessment, a topic that goes beyond the scope of this chapter.

Throughout this chapter, I have discussed replication studies as being essential to the growth of the discipline because they allow us to ask many different kinds of questions that are not available to most other types of research (e.g., revisiting a prior result, building confidence, adding nuance, exploring additional factors).

Replication studies encourage us November 5, 2026 Routledge Handbook of Second Language Acquisition Kevin McManus, kevin.mcmanus@pitt.edu to focus on a single study in a line of research with the aim to carefully consider its research design and methods, the types of results it generated, what those results mean, as well any implications arising from the study's results.

Furthermore, replication studies are key to cumulative knowledge building because no single study can possibly examine all relevant variables on a finding, so they allow researchers to build knowledge, refine and test theories, and further understanding in principled ways.
Replication studies are practically relevant because they allow us to build confidence around results before resources are used to invest in them (Tarone et al., 1976).
text.formatted: Replication studies are practically relevant because they allow us to build confidence around results before resources are used to invest in them <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Tarone et al., 1976)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, the field has witnessed debates about the relevance or impact of SLA research findings on classroom teaching for decades.
It has been repeatedly noted that replication studies are needed before we can begin to extend or apply SLA results to the classroom.
Why is this so?
Replication studies allow us to tease apart chance findings from observations that appear more stable.
SLA researchers are constantly developing new instructional approaches that build on prior work in diverse ways.
Replication studies allow us to build a case around a particular instructional technique.
In other words, replication allows us to better understand an instructional technique, when it appears to work, when it does not, and how it might vary across contexts.
These are critical steps to building confidence in a known finding or approach before extending and/or applying it.

It suggests that methodological limitations in the initial study may have impacted those early conclusions, but when these were ironed out different patterns of results began to emerge.
As this example shows, replication studies allow us to probe at the foundations of prior findings in principled ways.

text.text: In particular, replication allows us to invest in and scrutinize exploratory and sometimes faulty findings in a principled way before they are applied.

Lab-based studies Another reason that replication studies hold practical relevance is that they allow us to see how the results of lab-based studies (and online studies too) extend to other contexts in a principled way.
It is still the case that many types of SLA research are conducted in labbased contexts (e.g., outside of regular classroom time, without instructors).
While these studies hold important implications for L2 learning, the realities of authentic classrooms are quite different from the tightly controlled experimental conditions of the research lab.
Replication studies that repeat lab-based studies in the classroom have strong potential to tell us in what ways lab-based findings extend and can be used in the classroom.
What we tend to see is that instructional effects are much less pronounced in the classroom than in the lab, for several reasons.
For example, the populations studied in lab-based studies tend be relatively homogenous by design, whereas classroom studies include populations than are more diverse in all senses.
Similarly, lab-based research tends to reduce realworld distractions (e.g., completing a task in a sound-proof both), whereas classrooms can be full of many kinds of distractions.

These factors can make very clear effects from lab-November 5, 2026 Routledge Handbook of Second Language Acquisition Kevin McManus, kevin.mcmanus@pitt.edu 21 based research less impactful in the classroom, which highlight the relevance of replications for instruction.
A relevant to example to illustrate this point is Gass, Mackey and Ross-Feldman.
While not a replication study, the study set out to examine the ways in which L2 learners' task-based interactions compare in the classroom with the lab.

The study included university-level English-speaking learners of L2 Spanish who completed three interactive information exchange tasks (picture differences task, consensus task, and a map task) in dyads in a research lab context or an intact classroom context.

The results showed very few differences between the two contexts for three interactional features (negotiation for meaning, language-related episodes, and recasts), disagreeing with claims that the types of interactional features used in lab and classroom settings are not the same (e.g., Foster, 1998).

In this chapter , I have discussed and reviewed what replication studies are, what roles they play in the growth and development of the field, as well as recommended practices for replication study design and dissemination.
In this section, I outline future directions for replication studies in SLA.
First, replications should be integrated into existing programs of research program rather than one-off studies.

Similarly to research synthesis, replications can be November 5, 2026 Routledge Handbook of Second Language Acquisition Kevin McManus, kevin.mcmanus@pitt.edu 22 most useful at the beginning of a new line of research, including as part of graduate student training.
Replications play a central role in revisiting a key study to better understand its methods and aims, contextualize its findings, and inform future work in that line of research.
Through replication, researchers take away a much firmer understanding of work in that area and the nature of a previous study's methods and limits to the findings.
Doing replication research allows us to contribute to cumulative knowledge building in a principled way.
In addition, our decisions about what to replicate become intentional and principled and less opportunistic or idiosyncratic.
As reviewed in this chapter, the motivations for replication study designs are not always clear, but they need to be in order to better contribute to the field.
We can address this weakness by integrating replications into the regular workflow of research program development.

Second, there has been debate about the relevance and utility of replication studies outside of quantitative methods (Kim, 2025; Liu et al., 2026), which may have harmed the conduct of mixed-methods and qualitative replication studies.
text.formatted: Second, there has been debate about the relevance and utility of replication studies outside of quantitative methods <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Kim, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Liu et al., 2026)</ref>, which may have harmed the conduct of mixed-methods and qualitative replication studies.

text.text: It has been claimed that the aims of replication research are in tension with some of the aims and epistemological bases of qualitative and mixed-methods research.

For example, Casanave (2012) has argued that replication is suited to phenomena that are "relatively fixed or stable" (p. 297), adding that "if a replication is not as exact as possible, then it can hardly be called a replication" (p. 296).

text.text: In addition, Matsuda (2012) has argued that replication presupposes a world "that can be observed without any biases" (p. 300).
text.formatted: In addition, <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Matsuda (2012)</ref> has argued that replication presupposes a world "that can be observed without any biases" (p. 300).

text.text: As discussed in this chapter, replication studies allow one or more aspects of an earlier study to be revisited as way to corroborate, elaborate, contrast, or clarify.
Since all SLA research involves people, places, and objects that vary in space and time, there is no part of SLA that is fixed or stable.
On this view, intentionally varying or modifying one or more features of an earlier study is a defining part of the replication approach.
Aiming for exactness in replication is now widely understood to be unhelpful, unrealistic, and not achievable in human-subject research (Liu et al., 2026; Nosek & Errington, 2020).
text.formatted: Aiming for exactness in replication is now widely understood to be unhelpful, unrealistic, and not achievable in human-subject research <ref type="bibr">(Liu et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Nosek & Errington, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: For this reason, no replication study in SLA should expect or seek identical findings or context-free generalization.
What replication studies do allow, therefore, is an opportunity to study how a previous result or observation takes shape when it is studied again.

Going forward, it will be healthy and beneficial for the field to expand the use of replication beyond quantitative methods only, with appropriate recalibrations in line with a study's epistemological commitments.
Third, researchers should direct careful attention to replication study planning and reporting.
Both study planning and reporting have been reviewed in this chapter since both have strong potential to improve the quality of replication studies in the field.

When it comes to replication study planning, researchers are recommended to begin with the replication study planning questions provided in Appendix A. These questions can help researchers work through major components in the design of their replication, especially with regard to the value and impact of both the initial study and the replication.
In terms of study reporting, the reporting standard for replication studies in McManus (2024b) is a useful starting point.

The goal here is to assist researchers to more clearly (a) identify the study as a replication, (b) communicate the unique contributions of the study replication study, (c) describe all relevant similarities and differences between the studies, including design, methods, results, and (d) discuss the value and potential impact of the replication for the field.
The reporting standard walks researchers through each part of a study report so that the unique contributions of the replication can be clearly shared with the field.
Fourth, researchers are urged to fully share all materials, all data, and all analysis protocols and code.

Researchers were once encouraged to share their data collection materials, the research data, and their analysis protocols and/or code using trusted repositories like the Instruments for Research in Language Studies database (https://www.iris-database.org).
text.formatted: Researchers were once encouraged to share their data collection materials, the research data, and their analysis protocols and/or code using trusted repositories like the Instruments for Research in Language Studies database (<ref type="url" target="https://www.iris-database.org">https://www.iris-database.org</ref>).

text.text: Today, however, these open practices are now an expected component of the research process.
In other words, it is how we do research.
It is thus important that researchers take the necessary steps at study planning so that this important part of dissemination proceeds unhindered.
A study published today without open materials, open data, and open analysis protocols and/or code reduces its contribution to future scholarship.
For one, it is extremely difficult to replicate a study without open materials.
While some materials could be recreated, most cannot.
From my perspective, a study that does not have the potential to be replicated contributes little to the scientific record, no matter how unexpected or revolutionary the results.
In addition, I think that decisions about what to replicate should be based on data availability.
I see potential here more studies are making data available.
This will be an important step forward because it will allow replication studies to integrate analysis of the initial study's data into the full analysis of the replication.

This is a powerful resource for replication because it allows clearer statements and understandings about similarities and differences in the results, not only in terms of statistics, but also in terms of visualizations and even data coding.
The field has come a very long way in the conduct of replication studies in the last ten years.
We are beginning to see more published replications in the field.
More resources and methodological discussions about replication exist, which has likely made an important contribution to this change.
By engaging in this work, it is clear to see that we are beginning to be more rigorous and accountable not only in the topics we research, but also in how and why we do research.
These are healthy signatures for the future of our discipline.
